title: Syntax and structure of lambda expressions

blocks.text: 4.1.2. Syntax and Structure of Lambda Expressions
A shared messaging library adds a second way to register a handler, so that handlers can return an acknowledgement:

void onMessage(Consumer<Message> handler)      { ... }   // existing
void onMessage(Function<Message, Ack> handler) { ... }   // new
Three services upgrade and fail to compile on lines nobody changed:

Bus.java:17: error: reference to onMessage is ambiguous
        bus.onMessage(m -> audit.add(m.body()));
           ^
  both method onMessage(Consumer<Message>) in Bus and method onMessage(Function<Message,Ack>) in Bus match
`audit.add` returns a `boolean`, not an `Ack`. Why can't the compiler tell which overload fits? How a lambda gets its target type is unit 4.1.1; every output here is from Java 21.
A Lambda's Parameters Are All Inferred or All Declared
One list can't mix the forms:

Mixed.java:4: error: invalid lambda parameter declaration
    BinaryOperator<Integer> typedAndBare = (Integer a, b) -> a + b;
                                           ^
  (cannot mix implicitly-typed and explicitly-typed parameters)
Mixed.java:5: error: invalid lambda parameter declaration
    BinaryOperator<Integer> varAndTyped  = (var a, Integer b) -> a + b;
                                           ^
  (cannot mix 'var' and explicitly-typed parameters)
An annotation or `final` needs a declared type or `var`: `(@Trimmed s) -> s` and `(final s) -> s` are syntax errors. `var` exists to allow them, and still counts as inferred.
**Java 22 differs.** `(s, _) -> s` marks an unused parameter. Java 21 rejects it ("unnamed variables are a preview feature and are disabled by default"); it is standard from Java 22.
A Body's Shape Decides Whether It Returns a Value, Nothing, or Either

An expression body returns its value. A `void` target accepts only a statement expression (a method call, an assignment, `++`, `new Foo()`) and discards its value. So a call like `seen.add(...)` fits both kinds of target:

Runnable asRunnable       = () -> seen.add("a");      // the boolean is discarded
Callable<Boolean> asValue = () -> seen.add("b");      // the boolean is returned
call() = true, seen = [a, b]
A block body is void-compatible when no `return` in it carries a value, and value-compatible when every `return` carries one and control can't reach the closing brace. javac names each mismatch:

Incompatible.java:7: error: incompatible types: lambda body is not compatible with a void functional interface
    Runnable notAStatement   = () -> count + 1;
                                           ^
    (consider using a block lambda body, or use a statement expression instead)
Incompatible.java:8: error: incompatible types: bad return type in lambda expression
    Callable<Integer> noRet  = () -> { count++; };
                               ^
    missing return value
Incompatible.java:9: error: incompatible types: bad return type in lambda expression
    Function<String, Integer> somePaths = s -> {
                                          ^
    missing return value
Incompatible.java:13: error: incompatible types: bad return type in lambda expression
    Runnable returnsValue    = () -> { return count; };
                                              ^
    unexpected return value
`somePaths` falls off its end for a two-letter string. A block that can't reach its end and has no `return`, because it throws or loops forever, is both void- and value-compatible.
When a Body Fits Both, the Overload That Returns a Value Wins
`ExecutorService.submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` and `Callable`; `pick` copies that pair. Which overload does each call choose?

seen.add("x")                          -> Callable
{ seen.add("x"); }                     -> Runnable
System.out.println()                   -> Runnable
{ throw new IllegalStateException(); } -> Callable
{ while (true) { } }                   -> Callable
When a body fits both and its parameter types are known (declared, or there are none, as here), the compiler prefers the interface whose method returns a value. `submit` does the same:

pool.submit(() -> seen.add("o-7"))
pool.submit(() -> { seen.add("o-8"); })
pool.submit(() -> { archive("o-9"); return null; })   // archive(...) throws IOException

seen.add("o-7")                   get() = true
{ seen.add("o-8"); }              get() = null
{ archive("o-9"); return null; }  get() threw, cause = java.io.IOException: disk full while archiving o-9

Adding braces turned a `Future` holding `true` into one holding `null`. The third compiles only because `return null` makes it a `Callable`, whose `call()` may throw `Exception`. Without it javac picks `Runnable` and reports `unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown`. Catching it inside the lambda instead hides the failure or puts another exception in the `Future` (unit 3.2.2).
<!-- practice 1 -->
An Implicitly Typed Lambda Can't Choose Between Overloads of the Same Arity
Back to the library. With both `onMessage` overloads:

bus.onMessage(m -> audit.add(m.body()));       // ambiguous
bus.onMessage(m -> System.out.println(m));     // ambiguous
bus.onMessage(m -> ack(m));                    // ambiguous
bus.onMessage(m -> { audit.add(m.body()); });  // Consumer
bus.onMessage(m -> { return ack(m); });        // Function

`m`'s type depends on the overload being chosen, so for an implicitly typed lambda javac checks only the body's shape. An expression body might return a value, so it fits both, even `System.out.println(m)`. A block rules one out. Without declared types the value-returning preference doesn't apply, so the call is ambiguous. `(var m) -> ack(m)` is ambiguous too.

bus.onMessage((Message m) -> audit.add(m.body()));            // Consumer overload
bus.onMessage((Message m) -> ack(m));                         // Function overload
bus.onMessage((Consumer<Message>) m -> audit.add(m.body()));  // Consumer overload
bus.onMessageAck(m -> ack(m));                                // onMessageAck

Declared types let the compiler check the body: a `boolean` isn't an `Ack`, so only `Consumer` fits the first; `ack(m)` fits both, and the value-returning one wins. A cast names the target directly. These fix one call site; only a new name fixes every caller. The JDK's `comparingInt` and `mapToInt` are separate names: a replica that overloads `by(ToIntFunction)` and `by(Function)` makes `by(s -> s.length())` ambiguous.
A cast can also name several types, giving a lambda both interfaces:

plain: java.io.NotSerializableException
both:  written
A Lambda Can't Implement a Generic Method

Generic.java:6: error: incompatible types: invalid functional descriptor for lambda expression
    Picker larger = (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
                    ^
    method <T>(T,T)T in interface Picker is generic
  where T is a type-variable:
    T extends Comparable<T> declared in method <T>pick(T,T)
A lambda has nowhere to declare `<T>`. A method reference to a generic method fits, and so does an anonymous class:

static <T extends Comparable<T>> T larger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; }

Picker byRef = GenericRef::larger;   // byRef.pick("pear", "fig") is "pear", byRef.pick(3, 11) is 11
If each caller needs only one type, make the interface generic (`PickerOf<T>`) and a lambda fits.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Parameters are all inferred or all declared.** `var` allows annotations and `final`, but to overload resolution it is still inferred.
**A body's shape decides what it can return.** A statement expression that has a value fits both void and value targets; a block that can reach its end returns nothing.
**When a body fits both, the value-returning overload wins**, so braces can turn `submit(...).get()` from a value into `null`.
**An implicitly typed lambda can't choose between same-arity overloads.** Declared types or a cast fix one call; only a distinct method name fixes every caller.
**A lambda can't implement a generic method.** Use a method reference, a class, or a generic interface.

blocks.text: Reference
While overloads are chosen for an inferred lambda, every expression body counts as fitting both.
Challenges

items: Find an API in your codebase that overloads one name on two functional interfaces of the same arity. Which call sites compile only because of a block body or declared types?
You must add a value-returning variant to a published `register(Consumer<Event>)`. Compare a new name with a new handler interface.
A team rule says "always braces in lambdas". What does it change at run time?

blocks.text: Design Note: Overloads Are Chosen Before Inferred Bodies Are Checked

For an implicitly typed lambda, javac picks the overload from the arity and the shape of the body, and only then types the body, once, against one target. Typing it against every overload, with each candidate's parameter types, would multiply the work for nested lambdas, and an edit deep in a body could move the call to another method, which already happens for declared types. The price is this unit's ambiguity, and it falls on API designers.
